Nīlākṣa-nakula
(‘the blue-eyed mongoose’)
------------------------------------------
After the performance of the Aśva-medha sacrifice, king युधिष्ठिर, the eldest of the Pāṇḍavas, was puffed up with pride.
Suddenly, there appeared in the Yāgaśālā (sacrificial shed) a big mongoose with blue eyes, half of whose body had become golden. It rolled on the ground where there were scattered grains but seemed to be disappointed, since the other half too did not turn golden as it had hoped for. Then it spoke, like a human being, disparagingly of युधिष्ठिर’s so-called great sacrifice, comparing it with the sacrifice with life of a whole ब्राह्मण family out of hunger, after everyone of them gave away his or her share of ड़ोओद् to hungry souls who begged for the same. Accidental contact of the body of the mongoose with a small portion of the left-over ड़ोओद् in the ब्राह्मण’s होउसे had turned that half of its body into golden colour! Since that day the mongoose was trying to convert the other half of its body also into golden colour by visiting places where great sacrifices were being performed.
Naturally, युधिष्ठिर was humbled.

Nīlapurāṇa
------------------------------------------
If the number and the titles of the Mahāpurāṇas are fairly well-settled, those of the उपपुराणस् are not.
One of the उपपुराणस्, not listed among the traditional ones, but quoted by the writers of धर्मशास्त्रस् is the Nīla or the Nīlamatapurāṇa.
Though mentioned only in the Rāja-taraṅgiṇī of Kalhaṇa (12th cent. A. D.), it is a very interesting work, throwing a lot of light on the various aspects of Kashmir, like its history, legendary lores and topography.
While dealing with the दीपावली festival, it calls the Āśvina-अमावास्या (the new-मोओन् day of the month of Āśvina, in November) as ‘Śukhasuptikā’ and gives a grand, detailed description of its celebration. ड़स्तिन्ग् during the day, decorating temples with a long series of oil lamps, dressing oneself in new clothes and giving a good feast to the ब्राह्मणस् are the methods given for celebrating this festival.

Nīlakaṇṭha Dīkṣita
------------------------------------------
A famous and versatile author who enriched Sanskrit literature, नीलकण्ठ दीक्षित was the grandson of Accān Dīkṣiata who was a brother of another genius, अप्पय्य दीक्षित (A.

-1592). He lived in the 17th century.
Born as the son of नारायण Dīkṣita and Bhūmidevī at Aḍipala अग्रहार near the modern काञ्चीपुरम् (in Tamil Nadu), he acquired stupendous scholarship in several branches of learning like Mīmāṁsā, Vedānta, व्याकरण (grammar) and शैविस्म्.
His most famous work was Nīla-kaṇṭha-विजय-campū. Some of his other works are: Śivatattvarahasya, Śivalīlār-ṇava, Gaṅgāvataraṇa, Śāntivilāsa, Ānandasāgarastava, Nalacarita and Vairāgyaśataka.
The first of these works has expounded the Advaita Vedānta very well.

Nīlakaṇṭha
(‘one whose neck is blue’)
------------------------------------------
In the paurāṇic accounts of समुद्र-mathana or the churning of the ocean of milk, शिव is said to have gathered the poison हालाहल into his palm and drunk it. पार्वती, his spouse, pressed his throat so that the poison would not get into his stomach and destroy the worlds there. This poison stuck in his throat rendering his neck blue in colour. Hence शिव came to be known as ‘Nīlakaṇṭha,’ ‘one whose neck is blue’.
Nīlakaṇṭha is also the name of a Śaiva scholar from Maharashtra. He probably flourished in the middle of the 18th century. About six works are attributed to him, of which his commentaries on the Devībhāgavata and the Kātyāyanī Tantra are well-known.
A few more Nīlakaṇṭhas have been known to the students of the धर्म-śāstras as authors of various topics connected with the same.

Nīlakaṇṭha Caturdhara
------------------------------------------
The Mahābhārata, one of the two great epics of हिन्दुइस्म्, has a well-known commentary called Bhāratabhāvadīpa by नीलकण्ठ चतुर्धर. He was a descendent of one Lakṣmaṇārya, नारायण and Dhīreśa being two more distinguished ancestors of his.
